---
title: "Scalar-pretrain"
---

The scalar-pretrain setup keeps the architecture of ordinary causal language
model pretraining, including the native `lm_head`, but changes what supervision
is allowed to see. The underlying corpus token at each position is treated as a
hidden categorical state. The observed target is only a scalar label attached to
that token, currently the token id normalized to $[0, 1]$.

### TL; DR

::: {.callout-note}
All methods train a full LM from scratch and evaluate the same scalar prediction
metric over all $T = 128$ autoregressive positions. SL-CE observes the hidden
token ids and is the usual LM-pretraining upper reference. SL-LM-MSE does not
train on token ids; it directly optimizes the MSE of the softmax-projected
scalar mean. RLOO and GRPO, if they reward sampled hidden tokens by their scalar
MSE, optimize the expected sampled-token MSE, which differs from the evaluation
MSE by an extra model-variance term. Discrete MaxRL optimizes a log expected
scalar likelihood under the LM proposal; with a small label-likelihood
temperature it becomes CE-like, while with a large temperature it approaches the
same expected sampled-token MSE as RLOO.
:::

## Problem setup

Fix a corpus distribution $p$ over token sequences and a tokenizer vocabulary
$V$. In the canonical scalar-pretrain setting, each training row is a length
$T = 128$ token sequence
$$
Z_{1:T} \sim p,
$$
with a beginning-of-sequence token available as context for the first position.
At autoregressive position $i$, define
$$
C_i := (Z_0, Z_1, \dots, Z_{i-1}), \qquad Z_0 := \mathrm{BOS},
$$
so the model predicts the hidden current token $Z_i$ from its teacher-forced
prefix $C_i$. This gives $T$ supervised positions per row, not only the final
position.

The observed scalar label is a deterministic map
$$
\varphi : V \to [0, 1].
$$
For the current token-id label,
$$
Y_i := \varphi(Z_i), \qquad
\varphi(t) := \frac{t}{|V|}
$$

Every method uses the same causal transformer and the same native LM head. Let
the logits at position $i$ be
$$
a_{\theta, i}(t) \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad t \in V,
$$
and let the LM-head induced categorical distribution be
$$
q_{\theta, i}(t \mid C_i)
  := \frac{\exp a_{\theta, i}(t)}
          {\sum_{u \in V} \exp a_{\theta, i}(u)}.
$$
The scalar prediction used for evaluation is the softmax-projected mean
$$
\mu_{\theta, i}(C_i)
  := \mathbb{E}_{t \sim q_{\theta, i}(\cdot \mid C_i)}[\varphi(t)]
  = \sum_{t \in V} q_{\theta, i}(t \mid C_i)\,\varphi(t).
$$


## Canonical recipe

This is the proposed recipe, mirroring corpus-regression but changing the head
and the supervised positions.

| Knob | Proposed value |
|---|---|
| Backbone | Causal LM trained from scratch |
| Prediction head | Native `lm_head` for every method |
| Sequence length $T$ | 128 autoregressive target positions |
| Label | `token_id` normalized to $[0,1]$ |
| Scalar dimension | $D_y = 1$ |
| Training contexts | Teacher-forced token prefixes $C_i = Z_{<i}$ |
| Evaluation prediction | $\mu_{\theta,i} = \sum_t q_{\theta,i}(t)\varphi(t)$ |
| Main evaluation metric | MSE of $\mu_{\theta,i}$ against $Y_i$ |
| Normalization | MSE divided by empirical-mean baseline variance |
| Sampling methods | RLOO, GRPO, MaxRL with categorical LM proposal |
| Exact-limit variants | Replace rollout averages by full softmax sums over $V$ |

## Optimization problem and evaluation metric

### Population scalar objective

The evaluation target is the conditional expectation of the scalar label,
$$
\mu_i^\ast(C_i)
  := \mathbb{E}_{Z_i \sim p(\cdot \mid C_i)}[\varphi(Z_i)]
  = \sum_{t \in V} p(t \mid C_i)\,\varphi(t).
$$
The scalar MSE risk of a model is
$$
\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\theta)
  := \mathbb{E}_{Z_{1:T} \sim p}
      \left[
        \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}
        \bigl(\mu_{\theta,i}(C_i) - Y_i\bigr)^2
      \right].
$$
Conditioning on a prefix $C_i$, this decomposes as
$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
  \bigl(\mu_{\theta,i}(C_i) - Y_i\bigr)^2
  \,\middle|\, C_i
\right]
=
\bigl(\mu_{\theta,i}(C_i) - \mu_i^\ast(C_i)\bigr)^2
+ \mathrm{Var}\!\left(Y_i \mid C_i\right).
$$
Thus the Bayes-optimal scalar predictor is $\mu_i^\ast$, and the irreducible
Bayes lower bound is
$$
\mathbb{E}_{C_i}\,\mathrm{Var}(Y_i \mid C_i).
$$
The loss generally will not go to zero because the same prefix can lead to many
next-token labels.

### Held-out metric

For a validation batch with mask $m_{b,i} \in \{0,1\}$ and
$N = \sum_{b,i} m_{b,i}$ valid positions, use
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}
  = \frac{1}{N}
    \sum_{b,i} m_{b,i}
    \bigl(\mu_{\theta,i}(C_i^{(b)}) - Y_i^{(b)}\bigr)^2.
$$
For scalar labels $D_y = 1$. If this is later generalized to vector labels,
the natural extension is to average the squared error over both positions and
label dimensions.

The normalized metric should be
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{NMSE}}
  := \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}}{\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{mean}}},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{mean}}
  := \frac{1}{N}\sum_{b,i} m_{b,i}
       \bigl(Y_i^{(b)} - \bar Y\bigr)^2,
$$
where
$$
\bar Y := \frac{1}{N}\sum_{b,i} m_{b,i}Y_i^{(b)}.
$$
The denominator is exactly the held-out MSE of the constant empirical-mean
predictor, so that the mean baseline has normalized MSE $1$.

## Methods

The methods differ only in the training signal attached to the shared LM-head
distribution $q_{\theta,i}(\cdot \mid C_i)$. In the formulas below, suppress
batch and position indices and write
$$
q_t := q_\theta(t \mid C), \qquad
\phi_t := \varphi(t), \qquad
y := \varphi(z), \qquad
\mu_\theta(C) := \sum_{t \in V} q_t \phi_t.
$$

#### 4.1 Mean baseline - inference-only normalization

The constant baseline predicts
$$
\mu_0(C_i) := \bar Y_{\mathrm{train}}
$$
at every position. It does not train an LM and does not use the prefix. On the
validation split, if $\bar Y_{\mathrm{train}} \approx \bar Y_{\mathrm{val}}$,
its normalized MSE is approximately $1$ by construction.

This baseline is deliberately weak. It measures whether the LM has extracted
any useful scalar information from the prefix beyond the corpus-wide token-id
mean.

#### 4.2 SL-CE - ordinary LM pretraining with scalar evaluation

SL-CE is the vanilla supervised LM objective. It observes the hidden current
token id $Z_i$ and minimizes cross-entropy across all autoregressive positions:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}CE}}(\theta)
  = -\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1:T}\sim p}
      \left[
        \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}
        \log q_{\theta,i}(Z_i \mid C_i)
      \right].
$$
In minibatch form,
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}CE}}
  = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{b,i} m_{b,i}
      \log q_{\theta,i}(Z_i^{(b)} \mid C_i^{(b)}).
$$

Evaluation still uses only the scalar mean
$$
\mu_{\theta,i}(C_i)
  = \sum_{t \in V} q_{\theta,i}(t \mid C_i)\,\varphi(t),
$$
so SL-CE and scalar-only methods are compared in the same target space.

If $q_\theta(\cdot \mid C)$ converges to the true next-token distribution
$p(\cdot \mid C)$, then
$$
\mu_\theta(C) \to \sum_t p(t \mid C)\varphi(t) = \mu^\ast(C),
$$
which is Bayes-optimal for scalar MSE. Because token-id normalization is
injective on $V$, CE is strictly stronger supervision than scalar MSE: it tries
to recover the full hidden-token distribution, while the scalar metric only
cares about one expectation under that distribution.

#### 4.3 SL-LM-MSE - direct softmax-projected scalar MSE

SL-LM-MSE does not put CE loss on the hidden token id. It computes the full
LM-head distribution, projects it through the label map, and directly minimizes
the scalar prediction error:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}LM\mbox{-}MSE}}(\theta)
  = \mathbb{E}_{Z_{1:T}\sim p}
      \left[
        \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}
        \left(
          \sum_{t \in V} q_{\theta,i}(t \mid C_i)\varphi(t)
          - Y_i
        \right)^2
      \right].
$$
The minibatch estimator is exactly the held-out metric without the validation
split:
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}LM\mbox{-}MSE}}
  = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{b,i} m_{b,i}
      \bigl(\mu_{\theta,i}(C_i^{(b)}) - Y_i^{(b)}\bigr)^2.
$$

For one position, let the logits be $a_t$ and $q_t=\mathrm{softmax}(a)_t$.
Since
$$
\frac{\partial \mu}{\partial a_t}
  = q_t(\phi_t - \mu),
$$
the logit gradient is
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial a_t}(\mu - y)^2
  = 2(\mu - y)\,q_t(\phi_t - \mu).
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\nabla_\theta(\mu - y)^2
  =
  2(\mu-y)\,
  \mathbb{E}_{S\sim q_\theta}
  \left[
    (\varphi(S)-\mu)\,
    \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(S \mid C)
  \right].
$$

This is the clean scalar objective. It exactly targets the evaluation risk, but
it is a weaker training signal than CE. Many different token distributions can
have the same scalar mean, especially once the label is one-dimensional.

#### 4.4 RL common setup - categorical proposal over hidden tokens

For the RL-style methods, the LM head defines a proposal distribution over the
hidden current token:
$$
S_j \sim q_\theta(\cdot \mid C), \qquad j = 1,\dots,R.
$$
A natural scalar-MSE reward for a sampled hidden token is
$$
r(S_j; y) := -\bigl(\varphi(S_j) - y\bigr)^2.
$$
The exact expected reward under the LM proposal is
$$
J_{\mathrm{tok}}(\theta; C, y)
  := \mathbb{E}_{S\sim q_\theta}[r(S;y)]
  = -\sum_{t \in V} q_t(\phi_t-y)^2.
$$
The negative of this objective is
$$
-J_{\mathrm{tok}}
  = \sum_t q_t(\phi_t-y)^2
  = (\mu-y)^2 + \underbrace{\sum_t q_t(\phi_t-\mu)^2}
      _{\mathrm{Var}_{S\sim q_\theta}[\varphi(S)]}.
$$

This identity is the main conceptual distinction from SL-LM-MSE. Sampling a
hidden token and rewarding its scalar MSE does not optimize only the MSE of the
model-predicted mean. It also penalizes the variance of scalar labels under the
model's proposal distribution. Therefore, its optimum for a fixed observed
label is a concentrated distribution over tokens whose labels are near $y$,
not merely any distribution whose mean equals $y$.

#### 4.5 RLOO - leave-one-out sampled-token MSE rewards

For each position, draw $R \ge 2$ iid hidden-token rollouts
$$
S_1,\dots,S_R \sim q_\theta(\cdot \mid C),
$$
and compute rewards
$$
r_j := -(\varphi(S_j)-y)^2.
$$
The leave-one-out advantage is
$$
A_j
  := r_j - \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{k\ne j} r_k
  = \frac{R}{R-1}(r_j-\bar r),
\qquad
\bar r := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k=1}^{R} r_k.
$$
The score-function loss is
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RLOO}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{N R}
   \sum_{b,i}m_{b,i}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
   A_{b,i,j}\,
   \log q_{\theta,i}(S_{b,i,j} \mid C_i^{(b)}),
$$
with $A_{b,i,j}$ detached.

RLOO is an unbiased estimator of the expected sampled-token reward gradient.
Conditioned on peer samples $S_{-j}$,
$$
\mathbb{E}_{S_j}
\left[
  A_j \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(S_j \mid C)
  \,\middle|\, S_{-j}
\right]
=
\mathbb{E}_{S_j}
\left[
  r_j \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(S_j \mid C)
\right],
$$
because the peer baseline is independent of $S_j$ and
$\mathbb{E}_{S_j}\nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(S_j \mid C)=0$.

The no-sampling probability limit is obtained by replacing the rollout average
with the exact categorical expectation:
$$
J_{\mathrm{tok}}(\theta; C, y)
  = \sum_{t \in V} q_t r_t,
\qquad
r_t := -(\phi_t-y)^2.
$$
The exact advantage form is
$$
A_t^\infty := r_t - J_{\mathrm{tok}},
$$
and
$$
\nabla_\theta J_{\mathrm{tok}}
  =
  \sum_{t \in V} q_t A_t^\infty
  \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(t \mid C).
$$
Equivalently, the exact differentiable loss is
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RLOO}}^\infty
  := -J_{\mathrm{tok}}
  = \sum_{t \in V} q_t(\phi_t-y)^2
  = (\mu-y)^2 + \mathrm{Var}_{q_\theta}[\varphi(S)].
$$

Thus finite-$R$ RLOO estimates the gradient of the exact sampled-token-MSE
objective above. It does not estimate the gradient of SL-LM-MSE unless the
proposal variance term is zero or deliberately removed by changing the reward.

#### 4.6 GRPO - group-standardized sampled-token MSE rewards

GRPO uses the same categorical rollouts and rewards as RLOO,
$$
S_j \sim q_\theta(\cdot \mid C), \qquad
r_j = -(\varphi(S_j)-y)^2,
$$
but replaces the leave-one-out advantage with a group-standardized advantage:
$$
A_j
  := \frac{r_j-\bar r}{s_r+\epsilon},
\qquad
s_r^2 := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k=1}^{R}(r_k-\bar r)^2.
$$
The score-function loss is
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{N R}
   \sum_{b,i}m_{b,i}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
   A_{b,i,j}\,
   \log q_{\theta,i}(S_{b,i,j}\mid C_i^{(b)}),
$$
again with $A_{b,i,j}$ detached.

As in corpus-regression, finite-$R$ GRPO is not an unbiased estimator of the
plain REINFORCE gradient. The mean and standard deviation are computed from the
same group that contains $S_j$, so the score-function baseline is not cleanly
independent of the scored sample.

In the no-sampling limit, define
$$
J_{\mathrm{tok}} := \sum_t q_t r_t,
\qquad
\sigma_r^2 := \sum_t q_t(r_t-J_{\mathrm{tok}})^2.
$$
Then the limiting standardized advantage is
$$
A_t^\infty := \frac{r_t-J_{\mathrm{tok}}}{\sigma_r+\epsilon},
$$
and the limiting score-field is
$$
\sum_t q_t A_t^\infty \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(t\mid C)
  =
  \frac{1}{\sigma_r+\epsilon}
  \nabla_\theta J_{\mathrm{tok}}
$$
up to the $\epsilon$ stabilization. Therefore, when the reward variance is
nonzero, probability-exact GRPO points in the same direction as probability
exact RLOO, but rescales the step by the inverse reward standard deviation.

Implementation detail: the exact GRPO limit should be implemented as a detached
score-function surrogate, for example
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}^\infty
  =
  -\sum_t q_t\,\mathrm{stopgrad}(A_t^\infty),
$$
or equivalently with detached $q_tA_t^\infty$ multiplying $\log q_t$. Directly
differentiating a fully attached expression involving standardized advantages
does not reproduce the sampled GRPO estimator.

#### 4.7 MaxRL - discrete scalar-observation likelihood

MaxRL needs a nonnegative likelihood-like score for the observed scalar label
under each sampled hidden token. A natural choice is a Gaussian observation
likelihood in label space:
$$
\ell_y(t)
  :=
  \mathcal{N}\!\left(y;\,\phi_t,\tau^2\right)
  =
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\tau}
  \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\phi_t-y)^2}{2\tau^2}\right),
$$
with supremum
$$
L := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\tau}.
$$
The normalized likelihood is therefore
$$
\sigma_t(y)
  := \frac{\ell_y(t)}{L}
  =
  \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\phi_t-y)^2}{2\tau^2}\right)
  \in (0,1].
$$
Here $\tau$ is a label-likelihood temperature, not a rollout standard
deviation; the rollout distribution is categorical and comes entirely from the
LM head.

For one context-label pair, define the marginal normalized likelihood under the
LM proposal
$$
\sigma_\theta(C,y)
  := \mathbb{E}_{S\sim q_\theta(\cdot\mid C)}[\sigma_S(y)]
  = \sum_{t \in V} q_t\sigma_t(y).
$$
The degree-$M$ MaxRL population objective is the same Maclaurin truncation used
in [MaxRL gradient estimator details](gradient-estimator.qmd):
$$
J_M(\theta; C,y)
  :=
  -\sum_{k=1}^{M}\frac{(1-\sigma_\theta)^k}{k},
\qquad
w_M(\sigma_\theta)
  :=
  \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}(1-\sigma_\theta)^k.
$$
Its gradient is
$$
\nabla_\theta J_M
  =
  w_M(\sigma_\theta)
  \mathbb{E}_{S\sim q_\theta}
  \left[
    \sigma_S(y)\,
    \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(S\mid C)
  \right].
$$
With a baseline, this can also be written
$$
\nabla_\theta J_M
  =
  w_M(\sigma_\theta)
  \mathbb{E}_{S\sim q_\theta}
  \left[
    \bigl(\sigma_S(y)-\sigma_\theta\bigr)
    \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(S\mid C)
  \right].
$$

For a sampled degree $M$ estimator, require $1 \le M \le R$. The sampled
estimator draws $R$ hidden tokens
$$
S_1,\dots,S_R \sim q_\theta(\cdot\mid C),
$$
computes
$$
\sigma_j := \sigma_{S_j}(y), \qquad a_j := 1-\sigma_j,
$$
and forms the leave-one-out MaxRL weight
$$
\omega_j
  :=
  \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}
  \frac{
    e_k\bigl((a_\ell)_{\ell\ne j}\bigr)
  }{
    \binom{R-1}{k}
  },
$$
where $e_k$ is the $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial. This is exactly the
prefix-suffix dynamic program described in
[MaxRL gradient estimator details](gradient-estimator.qmd), specialized to a
categorical rollout distribution.

Without baseline subtraction,
$$
c_j := \omega_j\sigma_j.
$$
With the canonical leave-one-out baseline,
$$
c_j
  :=
  \omega_j
  \frac{R}{R-1}(\sigma_j-\bar\sigma),
\qquad
\bar\sigma := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k=1}^{R}\sigma_k.
$$
The sampled score-function loss is
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{MaxRL}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{N R}
   \sum_{b,i}m_{b,i}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
   c_{b,i,j}
   \log q_{\theta,i}(S_{b,i,j}\mid C_i^{(b)}),
$$
with $c_{b,i,j}$ detached.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Unbiasedness of the sampled estimator. 

Let
$$
G_R
  :=
  \frac{1}{R}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
  c_j\,\nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(S_j\mid C)
$$
be the stochastic gradient estimator for one context-label pair. First consider
the no-baseline coefficient $c_j=\omega_j\sigma_j$. For each $k$,
$$
\mathbb{E}
\left[
  \frac{
    e_k\bigl((a_\ell)_{\ell\ne j}\bigr)
  }{
    \binom{R-1}{k}
  }
\right]
=
\mathbb{E}_{I}
\mathbb{E}
\left[
  \prod_{\ell\in I}a_\ell
\right]
=
\bigl(\mathbb{E}[a]\bigr)^k
=
(1-\sigma_\theta)^k,
$$
where $I$ is a uniformly chosen $k$-subset of the $R-1$ peer rollouts. The
second equality uses iid peer rollouts. Therefore
$$
\mathbb{E}[\omega_j]
  =
  \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}(1-\sigma_\theta)^k
  =
  w_M(\sigma_\theta).
$$
Moreover, $\omega_j$ is a function only of the peer samples $S_{-j}$ and is
independent of $S_j$. Hence
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[G_R]
&=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
  \omega_1\sigma_1\nabla_\theta\log q_\theta(S_1\mid C)
\right] \\
&=
\mathbb{E}[\omega_1]\,
\mathbb{E}_{S\sim q_\theta}
\left[
  \sigma_S(y)\nabla_\theta\log q_\theta(S\mid C)
\right] \\
&=
w_M(\sigma_\theta)\,\nabla_\theta\sigma_\theta
=
\nabla_\theta J_M(\theta; C,y).
\end{aligned}
$$
The baseline-subtracted coefficient is unbiased for the same reason. Since
$$
\frac{R}{R-1}(\sigma_j-\bar\sigma)
  =
  \sigma_j-\bar\sigma_{-j},
\qquad
\bar\sigma_{-j}
  :=
  \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{\ell\ne j}\sigma_\ell,
$$
the baseline term obeys
$$
\mathbb{E}
\left[
  \omega_j\bar\sigma_{-j}
  \nabla_\theta\log q_\theta(S_j\mid C)
  \,\middle|\, S_{-j}
\right]
=
\omega_j\bar\sigma_{-j}
\mathbb{E}_{S_j}
\left[
  \nabla_\theta\log q_\theta(S_j\mid C)
\right]
=0.
$$
Thus leave-one-out baseline subtraction changes the variance but not the
expected gradient.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Unbiasedness of the Exact probability limit estimator.

The no-sampling limit is not a new stochastic
estimator. It is the same MaxRL population objective with the categorical
expectation evaluated exactly over the finite vocabulary:
$$
\sigma_\theta = \sum_t q_t\sigma_t(y).
$$
For finite degree $M$, one can directly maximize
$$
J_M(\theta; C,y)
  =
  -\sum_{k=1}^{M}\frac{(1-\sum_t q_t\sigma_t(y))^k}{k}.
$$
The chain rule gives
$$
\nabla_\theta J_M
  =
  w_M(\sigma_\theta)\nabla_\theta\sigma_\theta,
\qquad
w_M(\sigma_\theta)
  =
  \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}(1-\sigma_\theta)^k.
$$
Because $\sigma_t(y)$ is fixed with respect to $\theta$ for the observed
example,
$$
\nabla_\theta\sigma_\theta
  =
  \nabla_\theta\sum_t q_t\sigma_t(y)
  =
  \sum_t \sigma_t(y)\nabla_\theta q_t
  =
  \sum_t q_t\sigma_t(y)
     \nabla_\theta\log q_\theta(t\mid C).
$$
Subtracting the exact baseline $\sigma_\theta$ is valid because
$$
\sum_t q_t\nabla_\theta\log q_\theta(t\mid C)
  =
  \sum_t \nabla_\theta q_t
  =
  \nabla_\theta\sum_t q_t
  =
  0.
$$
Therefore the exact full-vocabulary score form is
$$
c_t^\infty
  =
  w_M(\sigma_\theta)\bigl(\sigma_t(y)-\sigma_\theta\bigr),
$$
and
$$
\nabla_\theta J_M
  =
  \sum_t q_t c_t^\infty
  \nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(t\mid C).
$$
This is the deterministic counterpart of the leave-one-out sampled estimator:
the peer-estimated $\omega_j$ has been replaced by its exact value
$w_M(\sigma_\theta)$, and the peer-estimated baseline has been replaced by the
exact marginal $\sigma_\theta$.

:::

There is no Gaussian-convolution identity here like in corpus-regression. The
proposal is categorical over hidden tokens, and the likelihood is a scalar
observation likelihood attached to each token. MaxRL's limit is therefore a
log expected scalar likelihood, not automatically the MSE of the projected
mean.

The temperature $\tau$ controls what this objective resembles:

- **Small $\tau$**. If $\varphi$ is injective and $y=\varphi(z)$, then
  $\sigma_z(y)\approx 1$ and $\sigma_t(y)\approx 0$ for $t\ne z$ when $\tau$
  is much smaller than the token-label spacing. Then
  $J_\infty \approx \log q_\theta(z\mid C)$, so MaxRL becomes CE-like. If
  $\varphi$ is non-injective, it instead maximizes the total probability of
  tokens sharing the observed label.
- **Large $\tau$**. Let $E_t=(\phi_t-y)^2$ and
  $\alpha=(2\tau^2)^{-1}$. Then
  $$
  \log\mathbb{E}_{t\sim q}\exp(-\alpha E_t)
  =
  -\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{t\sim q}[E_t]
  + \frac{\alpha^2}{2}\mathrm{Var}_{t\sim q}(E_t)
  + O(\alpha^3).
  $$
  To first order, maximizing MaxRL is equivalent to minimizing
  $\sum_t q_t(\phi_t-y)^2$, the same expected sampled-token MSE targeted by
  RLOO.

## Limit-behaviour summary

::: {.callout-note}
The exact softmax limit separates the methods cleanly:

| Method | Exact no-sampling target | Relationship to eval MSE |
|---|---|---|
| SL-CE | $\mathbb{E}_{p}[-\log q_\theta(Z_i\mid C_i)]$ | Stronger full-token supervision; Bayes-optimal scalar mean if $q_\theta\to p$ |
| SL-LM-MSE | $(\sum_t q_t\phi_t-y)^2$ | Exactly the scalar evaluation loss |
| RLOO | $\sum_t q_t(\phi_t-y)^2$ | Eval loss plus $\mathrm{Var}_{q_\theta}[\phi(S)]$ |
| GRPO | Whitened score field for RLOO target | Same limiting direction as RLOO, scaled by reward std |
| MaxRL | $\log\sum_t q_t\exp(-(\phi_t-y)^2/(2\tau^2))$ | CE-like for small $\tau$; RLOO-like to first order for large $\tau$ |
:::

The main practical implication is that SL-LM-MSE is the only scalar-only method
above that exactly optimizes the evaluation metric as written. The sampled-token
RL methods are still meaningful, but they answer a slightly different question:
how much probability mass does the LM proposal put on hidden tokens whose scalar
labels are compatible with the observed scalar label?

## Implementation notes

1. Compute logits with the standard causal shift over all 128 positions. The
   logits at context position $i-1$ predict $Z_i$.
2. Keep the native `lm_head` for every method. Do not replace it with a scalar
   regression head.
3. Build a label vector $\phi \in \mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ once and keep it on the
   active device. The projected scalar mean is `softmax(logits.float()) @ phi`.
4. For exact probability-limit RL variants, preserve the score-function
   gradient when using advantages. In particular, detach advantages in the
   probability-exact GRPO and MaxRL score surrogates.
5. Full `[batch, position, vocab]` probability tensors can be large. The exact
   variants may need vocab or position chunking, even though the mathematical
   formulation is just a finite sum over $V$.
6. Use the empirical-mean baseline variance for normalized MSE, but report raw
   MSE as well. The normalization is helpful for comparison, while raw MSE
   avoids hiding changes in label scaling.

## Open choices before implementation

- Choose the MaxRL label-likelihood temperature $\tau$. This is not a harmless
  constant: it determines whether MaxRL behaves more like CE or more like
  sampled-token MSE.
- Decide whether the primary RL comparison should use sampled-token-MSE rewards
  or the alternative score-function estimator that is unbiased for
  SL-LM-MSE itself.
